rv.q: Either way, the result is entertainment of an extremely high order: this is the kind of play that gives situation comedy its good name.
The first sight of director Claire Van Kampen's cleverly staged production is a visual knockout.
Mr. Jenkins’s language, moving like the flowing of a river through both the shallows and the depths, has a lightness of touch even when it is at its most plainly philosophical.

Nice Fish is certainly disjointed and rambling, and its slow pace could provoke irritation among the less patient. But its whimsical observational humor is consistently amusing, and the performers deliver the poetry with unforced naturalness.
Nice Fish has the flat, folksy vaudeville quality of that radio show, with its rime of humor and undertow of malaise.
Nice Fish is a whimsical, ultimately resonant portrait of lost souls waiting to hook or be hooked.
The whole may not add up to much more than a gently absurdist evocation of mood.
Featuring consummate performer Rylance himself in a company of five actors, this proves to be a charming and witty – though lighthearted – evening based on Jenkins’ wise and knowing prose poems.
Nice Fish, for all its characters’ expressions of regret at missing out, is a deeply warming, encouraging call for its audience to pay attention to and engage with life.
As it turns out, his work here is no fish story.
It's not much of a play, to be honest, but as a chance to relish the sublime eccentric charms of Rylance at his best, it's a hoot.
They bravely face life's futility with jokes, thoughtful observations, and the desire to simply catch a nice fish.
But there's a difference between performing poetry and transmuting it into theatrical action, and this is where the ice under Nice Fish starts to crack.
While there are moments that hook you and amuse and charm, the show, told in short scenes between blackouts in lieu of actual transitions, loses its grip.
It is around this point that Nice Fish completes its journey from amusing to bemusing to interminable.
But every moment of the play in which we’re denied Rylance’s presence – and there are too many of them – sags.
Unfortunately, the dreamy, meditative tone of Nice Fish is more likely to lull you into a gentle slumber than cause your ears to perk up in recognition of an artfully phrased truth.
Whatever, “Nice Fish” will not make you want to go out and buy Jenkins’s latest collection.

Alas, his Nice Fish, co-written with the poet Louis Jenkins, falls into the category of self-indulgent boondoggle (be it on a modest scale).

It’s filled with wit and charm to spare, a bit sad, and when it winds it’s way into an obscure abstract ending, Nice Fish brought a smile to my face and warmth to my heart, even on that cold cold lake.
Thanks to Rylance’s indomitable comedic spirit and Jenkins’s poetic words, Nice Fish offers a happier world view than Beckett’s – one that may send you up north to try ice-fishing yourself.
Nice Fish is funny and silly and touching. It slyly delivers laughs along with insights, so you never feel like your being lectured or on the lookout for the 'big answers'.
